While working on a larger data collection project, I ran into a recurring problem: downloading files was easy, but keeping track of what had been downloaded, verifying file integrity, and maintaining a clear record of the process was much less convenient.

That's why I started developing DataHarvester.
DataHarvester is a portable Windows application designed to collect files from public HTTPS sources while providing integrity verification and traceable reports.

articles.author: Ashish
articles.description:
De la vis d'Archimède au moteur moléculaire : pourquoi j'ai cessé de regarder les protéines sur écran plat pour entrer dedans (VR/Quest)


J'ai passé des nuits entières à tourner des modèles 3D sur un moniteur 27 pouces, à zoomer, pivoter, couper — et à ressentir cette frustration sourde : la profondeur reste une illusion. Quand j'ai enfilé mon Quest 2 pour la première fois avec une application de visualisation moléculaire open‑source (basée sur Unity + OpenXR), le changement a été brutal. Le casque rend la stéréoscopie native, le suivi 6 DoF sans marqueurs, et le passthrough vidéo me permet de garder un œil sur mon clavier tout en manipulant une ribosome à taille réelle.
Côté architecture, le pipeline est simple : les fichiers PDB/ mmCIF sont parsés en C# (Bio.NET), transformés en Mesh GPU via Compute Shaders, puis streamés vers le compositor Quest à 72 fps. Le gros gain vient du instanced rendering pour les résidus répétés ; sur mon Snapdragon XR2 j'obtiens ~1,2 M triangles à 90 fps sans thermal throttling. J'ai benchmarké la même scène sur Desktop (RTX 3080) : 3,8 M triangles, mais la latence tête‑à‑écran reste ~30 ms contre 12 ms en standalone. Le compromis ? Perdre le ray‑tracing temps‑réel, gagner la mobilité et l'immersion totale.
Le moment « aha » est arrivé un soir d'hiver, café fumant à la main, quand j'ai pu « marcher » le long du tunnel d'une polymérase, sentir la tension des liaisons hydrogène sous mes doigts virtuels. Ce n'est pas une démo marketing ; c'est le fruit d'un pipeline que j'ai moi‑même assemblé, testé, optimisé. Aujourd'hui, chaque nouvelle structure que je charge devient une promenade, pas une diapositive.
Si vous codez en C#/Unity et voulez sortir du plat, essayez le SDK OpenXR pour Quest — la courbe d'apprentissage est courte, le retour visuel immédiat. 🚀
articles.title: De la vis d'Archimède au moteur moléculaire : pourquoi j'ai cessé de regarder les protéines sur écran plat pour entrer dedans…

articles.author: An Nguyễn Hoàng
articles.description:
Ask Claude or Cursor "is this GitHub repo still maintained?" and it does the only thing it can from a chat box: fetch the README and guess. The README is marketing. It won't tell you that one file has been rewritten nine times in the last twenty commits, that CI is mostly green-by-skip, or that three of the top five contributors stopped pushing a year ago.
That gap — the repo's behaviour versus the repo's description — is exactly the kind of thing an MCP tool can close, because it needs live API calls the model can't make on its own. So I built a small remote MCP server that does six read-only things against any public repo and hands the agent back clean structured JSON.
get_repo_overview — stars, forks, language, license, topics, last push
list_recent_prs — recent PRs with author, state, …
articles.title: Your coding agent can read a GitHub repo's vibe, not just its README

You write a README in VS Code, check the preview, push, and the repo page looks different. Sometimes better: the checkboxes you typed are real checkboxes now. Sometimes it goes the other way, and the note you were proud of in the preview turns out to need syntax the preview never understood.
The reason is simple. GitHub and VS Code use different Markdown renderers, and each one supports a different set of extras on top of the basics. We rendered the same README through both to see exactly where they split.
We wrote one README with every feature people reach for: an alert, a task list, a table, inline math, a Mermaid diagram, a footnote and a collapsible <details> block. Then we rendered it two ways on October 30, 2026:
GitHub: through GitHub's own Markdown API in gfm mode, the same rendere…

articles.author: Paradox
articles.description:
Before someone sends you a convincing phishing email, they do their homework. They look up your email address, find which accounts it's linked to, and use that to write a message that sounds real.
I wanted to see that homework from the attacker's side. So I ran my own email address through SpiderFoot, a free OSINT tool, on my Kali machine.
This post shows how to do the same for yourself: setup, running the scan, reading the results, and the cleanup checklist I'd follow afterwards.
Ground rule: only scan targets you own or have written permission to test. Your own email, your own usernames, your own domain. That's the whole point of this guide.
SpiderFoot is an open-source OSINT automation tool. You give it a target (an email address, username, domain, IP address or name) and it queries 200…
articles.title: I Ran My Own Email Through SpiderFoot. Here's What an Attacker Would See (and How to Check Yours)

articles.author: Swipe Again
articles.description:
A few years ago, "failed payment recovery" was a paragraph inside a churn tool's feature list. It now has its own category name, its own comparison pages, and — inevitably — its own marketing inflation. Products that send two reminder emails and retry on the processor's default schedule present themselves as recovery platforms. Products that genuinely conduct a recovery sequence present themselves the same way. From the buyer's chair, the pages look identical. The implementations are not.
Strip the language down and the thin end of the category does exactly two things: it watches for a failed charge, and it emails the subscriber a link. The retries themselves belong to Stripe or the billing platform, on their schedule, with their logic. This is not worthless — a decent email beats no email…
articles.title: The Category Has a Name Now. Most of It Is Still One Feature Wearing a Suite's Clothes
